title: Why isn't my CORS configuration causing the server to filter incoming requests? How can I make the server only accept requests from a specific origin?
ground_truth_answer:
CORS configuration won’t prevent the server from accepting requests based on the value of the Origin request header. You can’t do that just through CORS configuration.

When you configure CORS support on a server, all that the server does differently is just to send the Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header and other CORS headers.

Enforcement of CORS restrictions is done only by browsers. It’s not enforced by servers.

CORS works like is: regardless of any CORS config you make on the server side, the server continues accepting requests from all clients and origins it otherwise would; and so all clients from all origins continue getting responses from the server just as they otherwise would.

So even when you see an error in browser devtools that a cross-origin request from your frontend JavaScript code failed, you’ll still be able to see the response in browser devtools.

But just because your browser can see the response doesn’t mean the browser will expose it to your frontend code. Browsers only expose responses for cross-origin requests to frontend code running at a particular origin if the server the request went to opts-in to allowing the request by responding with an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header which OKs that origin.

So for any requests with an Origin request header matching https://foreign.domain, the configuration snippet in the question should cause browsers to emit a message on the client side saying http://localhost:3000/api/v1/bodies.json can’t be loaded because there’s no Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header in the response (because your configuration causes the server to only send that header in responses to your whitelisted origins).

But that’s all you can do through CORS. You can’t prevent the server side from accepting and responding to requests from particular origins just by doing any CORS configuration on the server side. If you want to do that, you need to do it using something other than just CORS.

Q: CORS Error: “requests are only supported for protocol schemes: http…” etc A:

XMLHttpRequest cannot load localhost:4201/ticker. Cross origin requests are only supported for protocol schemes: http, data, chrome, chrome-extension, https.

Any time you see that “only supported for protocol schemes” message, it almost certainly means you’ve just forgotten to put the https or http on the request URL in your code.

So in this case, the fix is to use the URL http://localhost:4201/ticker in your code here:

this._baseUrl = 'http://localhost:4201/';

…because without the http:// there, localhost:4201/ticker isn’t really the URL you intend.

Q: Using rack-cors with Rackspace CDN issues A:

To get CORS working properly, you'll need to set the CORS headers on the Cloud Files object on Rackspace's end, rather than the ones served by your app. You can do this from the control panel by clicking on the gear icon next to each file:

The Cloud Files documentation includes a section on the CORS headers that are supported and what each means.

If you have a large number of assets, or a build process that publishes them automatically, you'll want to use the API or an SDK to set these instead. The developer documentation includes a code snippet that you can adopt to do this; substitute "Access-Control-Allow-Origin" or the other relevant headers for "Content-Type".

Here's a complete example using the Ruby SDK, Fog:

require 'fog'

# Authenticate
@client = Fog::Storage.new(
  :provider => 'rackspace',
  :rackspace_username => '{username}',
  :rackspace_api_key => '{apiKey}',
  :rackspace_region => '{region}'
)

# Find the file object
@directory = @client.directories.get("{container name}")
@file = @directory.get("{file name}")

#

Q: Perform HTTP OPTIONS request from Rails 5 for CORS pre-flight or otherwise A:

At the top of your config/routes.rb file place the following:

match "/example/",
  controller: "example_controller",
  action: "options_request",
  via: [:options]

And in your controller write:

def options_request
  # Your code goes here.
end

If you are interested in writing an integration test there is some misinformation around the process method, which is not actually a public method. In order to support OPTIONS requests from your integration tests create an initializer (mine is at: config/initializers/integration_test_overrides.rb because I override a number of things) and add the following code:

class ActionDispatch::Integration::Session

  def http_options_request(path)
    process(:options, path)
  end

end

So that you can call http_options_request from your integration test.

Q: Can't render iframe on another domain using rack-cors A:

I am not sure if this is specifically to rack-cors, but I do know that the header 'X-Frame-Options' is intentionally set to 'sameorigin' for at least Rails 5. Most likely to prevent developers from unintentionally allowing someone to wrap their server in an iframe.

According to the docs, we can see that if the server sets this response as not 'sameorigin', then the browser will allow the HTML code to run. So what we need is to remove that header away. Chris Peters does a great job at this post. To save a click

class SomeController < ApplicationController
  after_action :allow_iframe

  
  private

  def allow_iframe
    response.headers.except! 'X-Frame-Options'
  end
end

To apply this to all endpoints simply place the after_action line and the function code in the application controller, but I would suggest limiting this to only specific pages/controllers.

llm_answer:
The issue you're encountering with your CORS configuration is due to a misunderstanding of how CORS works in your setup. The error message "requests are only supported for protocol schemes: http, data, chrome, chrome-extension, https" suggests that your server is interpreting "localhost:3000" as a protocol, but it should be interpreted as a domain. Therefore, you need to provide the protocol scheme explicitly in your CORS configuration.

To fix this, you should modify your CORS configuration to include the protocol scheme (`http` or `https`) in the allowed origins. Here’s how you can do it:

1. Ensure your `config/initializers/cors.rb` file contains the following lines:

```ruby
Rails.application.config.middleware.insert_before 0, Rack::Cors do
  allow do
    origins "http://localhost:8888" # Use http or https based on your needs
    resource "*", headers: :any, methods: [:get, :post, :put, :patch, :delete, :options, :head]
  end
end
```

2. Make sure you have the `rack-cors` gem installed in your Gemfile:

```ruby
gem 'rack-cors'
```

And run:

```bash
bundle install
```

3. Ensure your `config/environments/development.rb` (and other environments if necessary) have the following middleware configuration:

```ruby
config.middleware.insert_before 0, Rack::Cors do
  allow do
    origins "http://localhost:8888" # Use http or https based on your needs
    resource "*", headers: :any, methods: [:get, :post, :put, :patch, :delete, :options, :head]
  end
end
```

4. When testing, ensure your test requests include the correct headers. For example:

```ruby
#/spec/request/cors_request_spec.rb

RSpec.feature "CORS protection", type: :request do
  it "should accept a request from a whitelisted domain" do
    get "/api/v1/bodies.json", nil, "HTTP_ORIGIN": "http://localhost:8888"
    expect(response.status).to eql(200)
  end
  it "should reject a request from a non-whitelisted domain" do
    get "/api/v1/bodies.json", nil, "HTTP_ORIGIN": "https://foreign.domain"
    expect(response.status).to eql(406)
  end
end
```

5. Run the test and check the response. If the test fails, you need to ensure that your server is correctly interpreting the request headers. You can do this by checking your server logs or by inspecting the request headers using tools like `curl` or browser developer tools.

By following these steps, you should be able to allow only requests from your specified origin (`http://localhost:8888`) and reject requests from other domains. This should resolve the issue with the failing CORS request test.

Q: Object oriented design? A:

There are many 'mindsets' that you could adopt to help in the design process (some of which point towards OO and some that don't). I think it is often better to start with questions rather than answers (i.e. rather than say, 'how can I apply inheritance to this' you should ask how this system might expect to change over time).

Here's a few questions to answer that might point you towards design principles:

  • Are other's going to use this API? Are they likely to break it? (info hiding)
  • do I need to deploy this across many machines? (state management, lifecycle management)
  • do i need to interoperate with other systems, runtimes, languages? (abstraction and standards)
  • what are my performance constraints? (state management, lifecycle management)
  • what kind of security environment does this component live in? (abstraction, info hiding, interoperability)
  • how would i construct my objects, assuming I used some? (configuration, inversion of control, object decoupling, hiding implementation details)

These aren't direct answers to your question, but they might put you in the right frame of mind to answer it yourself. :)

import csv
from io import StringIO
from collections import UserList
from typing import Iterable, Mapping

from pydantic import ValidationError

from models.ValidTransaction import ValidTransaction

class CSVFile:
    class ValidTransactions(UserList):
        def to_csv(self) -> str:
            output = StringIO()
            header = ValidTransaction.get_output_header()
            writer = csv.DictWriter(output, header)
            writer.writeheader()
            
            for tx in self.data:
                writer.writerow(tx)

            return output.getvalue()

    def __init__(self, rows: Iterable[Mapping]) -> None:
        self.valid_transactions: CSVFile.ValidTransactions = self.ValidTransactions()
        
        for row in rows:
            valid_tx = ValidTransaction(**row)
            self.valid_transactions.append(valid_tx.dict())

Q: Design classes - OOPS features A:

  1. Encapsulation: The wrapping up of data and functions into a single unit is known as encapsulation. Or, simply put: putting the data and methods together in a single unit may be a class.

  2. Inheritance: Aquiring the properties from parent class to child class. Or: getting the properties from super class to sub class is known as inheritance.

  3. Polymorphism: The ability to take more that one form, it supports method overloading and method overriding.

    Method overloading: When a method in a class having the same method name with different arguments (diff parameters or signatures) is said to be method overloading. This is compile-time polymorphism – using one identifier to refer to multiple items in the same scope.

The problem you're encountering is that the Checkbook object is not being used effectively as expected. In your current implementation, you're using `ledger` as a list to store the transactions, but `Checkbook` objects should be used to encapsulate the transaction logic and maintain the state of the checkbook.

Here's a more OOP-friendly approach to your code:

1. **Refactor `Checkbook` to use a `Transaction` class**: This will allow you to encapsulate the logic for each transaction within the `Checkbook` class. This will also make it easier to add new types of transactions in the future.

2. **Use `transaction` objects**: This will allow you to manage the transaction process more effectively and keep the state of the checkbook.

Here's how you can refactor your code:

```python
import sys
import time

# Define the transaction types
class Debit:
    def __init__(self, payee, amount):
        self.payee = payee
        self.amount = amount

class Credit:
    def __init__(self, source, amount):
        self.source = source
        self.amount = amount

# Define the checkbook class
class Checkbook:
    def __init__(self, payees, sources):
        self.payees = payees
        self.sources = sources
        self.transactions = []

    def add_transaction(self, transaction):
        self.transactions.append(transaction)

    def get_transactions(self):
        return self.transactions

# Define the main transaction function
def process_transactions():
    while True:
        choice = input('Posting debit [d], credit [c] or [x] to exit: ')
        if choice == 'x': break

        if choice == 'd':
            payee = input('Check Number: ')
            trans_date = input('Transaction Date: ')
            source = input('Source: ')
            amount = input('Amount: ')
            memo = input('Memo (or Enter to skip): ')
            check = Debit(payee, amount)
            ledger.append(check)
            process_transactions()
        elif choice == 'c':
            source = input('Check Number: ')
            trans_date = input('Transaction Date: ')
            source = input('Source: ')
            amount = input('Amount: ')
            memo = input('Memo (or Enter to skip): ')
            check = Credit(source, amount)
            ledger.append(check)
            process_transactions()
        else:
            print("Invalid input. Please choose [d] or [c].")

# Example usage
if __name__ == "__main__":
    payees = ["Payee1", "Payee2"]
    sources = ["Source1", "Source2"]
    checkbook = Checkbook(payees, sources)
    ledger = []

    while True:
        process_transactions()
        time.sleep(1)  # Simulate delay for better user experience
```

### Explanation:
1. **Transaction Types**: We have defined two classes `Debit` and `Credit` to encapsulate the logic for each type of transaction.
2. **Checkbook Class**: The `Checkbook` class now manages a list of transactions. Each transaction is an instance of `Debit` or `Credit` classes.
3. **Main Transaction Function**: The `process_transactions` function is called recursively to simulate the process of checking and posting transactions.

This approach keeps your code more organized and easier to manage, especially as you grow more complex with your checkbook system.

title: Order <li> elements by id from array
ground_truth_answer:
Easiest way is to let PHP handle your order when loading the page. If not possible, because you'll only have the values in an array, it can be done by jQuery.

Do you have the jQuery code into the html/php page? Then you can do something like:

    <script>
        var sorted = <?= $sortOrderArray; ?>
        sorted.forEach(function(id) {
            $("#" + id).appendTo("#sortable")
        })
    </script>

I wouldn't recommend this because I preferably do not want JS/jQuery in my HTML/PHP.

title: Change the result that shown in a table
ground_truth_answer:
You can check the value of $row['result'] inside the while($row = mysqli_fetch_array($result)) block and display the content of <td> accordingly

while($row = mysqli_fetch_array($result))
{
    echo "<tr align='center'>";
    echo "<td width=10%>" . $row['id_get'] . "</td>";
    echo "<td width=10%>" . $row['trans_id'] . "</td>";
    if ($row['result'] == '1') {
        echo "<td width=10%>Accepted</td>";
    }
    else if ($row['result'] == '2') {
        echo "<td width=10%>Rejected</td>";
    }
    else {
        echo "<td width=10%>Unknown</td>";
    }
    echo "</tr>";
}

or alternatively you can change your query to this

$result = mysqli_query($conn,"SELECT id_get, trans_id, (CASE WHEN result = 1 THEN 'Accepted' WHEN result = 2 THEN 'Rejected' ELSE 'Unknown' END) AS result_description FROM users");

and simply display $row['result_description']

while($row = mysqli_fetch_array($result))
{
    echo "<tr align='center'>";
    echo "<td width=10%>" . $row['id_get'] . "</td>";
    echo "<td width=10%>" . $row['trans_id'] . "</td>";
    echo "<td width=10%>" . $row['result_description'] . "</td>";
